source.title: Is More Data Worth the Cost? Dataset Scaling Laws in a Tiny Attention-Only Decoder
source.authors: Götz-Henrik Wiegand; Lorena Raichle; Rico Städeli; T. Hrycej; Bernhard Bermeitinger; Siegfried Handschuh

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Figures are referenced, but their plotted data values are not available in the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: It measures validation loss across dataset sizes in a controlled, reduced architecture, but does not reproduce the original broad parameter/data/compute scaling sweeps or fit the original laws.
record.gate_note: The paper tests dataset-size effects with a fixed-capacity model, using both a fixed-epoch schedule and a fixed-optimization-step regime. Its Kaplan-law calculation is a reference prediction using reported constants, not a fit to its own small runs. The text describes figure-level trends but does not expose individual plotted loss values.
record.test_reason: The study trains a tiny attention-only GPT-2 decoder (2.36M trainable parameters, frozen embeddings, no MLPs) on nested data subsets from 0.13M to 134M tokens. It reports held-out cross-entropy against dataset size under fixed-epoch and fixed-step schedules, and compares the curve with a Kaplan-constant prediction. That is a new setting with a result on data scaling (V1) and on schedule dependence (V7). It fits no power law of its own.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that validation performance improves smoothly with data, with clear diminishing returns, in a tiny attention-only decoder. They say the model is data-limited rather than capacity-limited, so the architectural reductions do not alter scaling behaviour. They attribute earlier-than-predicted saturation to the finite fixed-epoch budget. Their practical claims are that about 30% of the data gives about 90% of full-data accuracy, and that subset pretraining with early stopping is efficient.
record.recipe_differences: Measures held-out language-model cross-entropy while scaling dataset size, but uses a tiny attention-only GPT-2-based decoder, fixes model capacity, and compares fixed-epoch and fixed-step schedules rather than conducting broad jointly fitted parameter/data/compute sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: The observed curve differs between fixed-epoch and fixed-optimization-step regimes; the authors also note that larger datasets are comparatively undertrained under fixed-epoch training.

fits_no_version.finding: About 29-30% of the data reaches about 90% of full-data validation token accuracy, at 26% of training cost (Table 3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under a fixed epoch schedule, most attainable validation accuracy of a tiny LM is reached with a small fraction of the data.

record.peer_reviewed: Presented as a paper at 3rd DATA-FM workshop @ ICLR 2026; peer-review status not stated in the text.
record.problems: The tested architecture is highly reduced and uses frozen pretrained embeddings/output weights. The main experiment uses one random seed; multi-seed results are reported only at epoch 1 for selected subset sizes. The main loss curves are not numerically tabulated in the supplied text, and the authors say the fixed-epoch runs do not ensure convergence. The comparison uses previously reported Kaplan constants rather than fitting and validating an extrapolation on the study's own small runs.
record.rows_left_out: None. Figure-level rows record only the overall trends described in the text because individual plotted values are unavailable in the supplied text.

untested.parts: Parameter-count and compute scaling; any fitted power law or exponent; loss with compute not the bottleneck at converged training.
All parts: no laws are fitted on small runs and used to predict larger runs.
All parts: token accuracy on the validation set is not a downstream task.
Parameter counting, data choice and fitting method are not varied; the schedule effect is the authors' attribution, not a controlled comparison of converged runs.

missing.what: Kaplan reference numbers for the full data: predicted L≈3.46 nats/token, L(N,∞)≈2.96, L(∞,D)≈3.37, with N=40M non-embedding parameters. These are a computed reference, not measured results, but the empirical best losses to compare with them are not given in text.

record.verdict_notes: Main runs use a single seed; T5 multi-seed values are epoch-1 only and mainly show sampling robustness. The Kaplan comparison counts 40M parameters including frozen weights versus 2.36M trainable, which makes the 'data-limited' conclusion depend on parameter counting. The authors themselves call the comparison qualitative. Peer review is a workshop paper.

versions.untested_parts: Only dataset-size scaling is tested. Parameter-count and compute scaling with the other factors independently varied, and a quantitative power-law fit over the tested range, are not reported.

The study does not fit laws on its own small runs and use those fits to predict substantially larger runs. It compares its empirical curve with a prediction using previously reported Kaplan constants.
No loss-minimising parameter/token allocation is found or tested as a function of compute.
Architecture details are held fixed; depth, width, and other architecture choices are not compared at a fixed parameter count.
No other modalities, repeated-data regimes, fine-tuning, or transfer settings are tested.
No downstream task performance is measured.
The study reports a deviation associated with its fixed-epoch training schedule, but does not systematically vary parameter counting, dataset choices, or fitting methods/exponents.

rows.subject: attention-only architecture (GPT-2-based)
rows.operation_detail: Validation loss measured at epoch 1 across subset sizes; five-seed mean and standard deviation reported.
rows.note: Reported as mean ± standard deviation over five seeds.
rows.check: This row is from a seed-robustness check (Table 5) at epoch 1. Steps grow with subset size, so data and compute co-vary. Losses (11.24 down to 6.34, perplexity up to 76k) are far from trained levels, and no fit is made, so it cannot show a power law in data. The same applies to all T5 rows.

rows.operation_detail: Validation cross-entropy measured across training subset sizes under a fixed 150-epoch schedule.

conditions.value: 150 epochs; compute increases with subset size

rows.note: The text describes early improvements followed by diminishing returns and saturation; individual curve values are not present in the supplied text.
rows.check: The state is acceptable. Loss falls with diminishing returns and then saturates beyond moderate subsets. No power-law fit is given, and under fixed epochs data and compute co-scale. Values are figure-only.

source_check.correct: For V1, state=cannot_determine. The reported curve shows diminishing returns under jointly increasing data and compute; convergence is not ensured and no power-law fit is reported.
source_check.problem: Partial overstates what this experiment establishes about V1 under its non-bottleneck conditions.

rows.subject: attention-only architecture (GPT-2-based)
rows.size_stated: approximately 40 million parameters for the Kaplan comparison; 2,361,600 trainable parameters in the experimental architecture
rows.operation_detail: Empirical best validation cross-entropy per subset is compared with a prediction from the Kaplan scaling-law equation.

conditions.value: fixed epochs; larger subsets described as comparatively undertrained
Kaplan joint-fit constants reported in the paper

rows.measure: Empirical best validation cross-entropy versus predicted test loss
rows.baseline: Kaplan scaling-law prediction; predicted loss at full-data scale is approximately 3.46 nats/token
rows.note: The text says the empirical curve saturates substantially earlier than the prediction, while still describing additional-data gains as following the expected power-law trend. Individual plotted values are not available in the supplied text.
rows.check: Authors say the curve follows the expected power-law trend but saturates substantially earlier than predicted. For V7 this is a bend attributed to the schedule. The prediction uses N≈40M parameters (all non-embedding, including frozen) although only 2.36M are trainable, a parameter-counting choice the paper does not examine.

source_check.correct: V1: cannot_determine because convergence and non-bottleneck conditions are not established. V7: observed for the reported curve departure attributed to the training schedule. Section 6.3 uses N≈40 million and predicts full-data loss≈3.46 nats/token.
source_check.locator_found: Section 6.3, equations 3–7 and following discussion; Appendix C, Figure 6.
source_check.problem: A shared partial state conflates an inconclusive V1 test with the reported V7 curve departure; the prediction's parameter count also conflicts with the architecture description.

relationships.condition: Fixed 150-epoch data sweep, tiny attention-only decoder, All the News 2.0
relationships.reason: Loss falls with data but saturates well before the Kaplan prediction; no power law is fitted and the larger subsets are undertrained (F4, F6).
relationships.display_finding: Loss decreased with more data but saturated well before the Kaplan prediction, while larger subsets remained undertrained.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Fixed 150-epoch data sweep, tiny attention-only decoder, All the News 2.0
source_check.reason: F4 and F6 do not establish V1's non-bottleneck conditions. Earlier saturation under acknowledged incomplete convergence does not require qualifying a claim already conditional on sufficient compute and capacity.

relationships.reason: The data-scaling curve bends away from the Kaplan curve, which authors attribute to the schedule. Under fixed steps the largest subsets stop improving (F6, F7). The attribution is not separately controlled.
relationships.display_finding: The largest subsets stopped improving under fixed steps, and the data curve departed from the Kaplan curve; the authors attributed this to scheduling without separately controlling that explanation.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.reason: Section 6.3 reports earlier saturation than the Kaplan reference and attributes it to training regime; Section 6.2 reports no consistent gains for the largest subsets under fixed steps. Supports the curve-bending component only; exponents and compute-optimal allocation are untested, and the causal attribution is not independently established.

relation.reason: Measures held-out loss across dataset sizes and training schedules and compares its empirical curve with a scaling-law reference.

tranche.reason: Reports dataset-scaling results in a tiny attention-only decoder with frozen pretrained embeddings, a new setting bearing on schedule-dependent curve behavior.

source_check.notes: Section 6.3 uses approximately 40M non-embedding parameters, whereas Table 1 reports 79,556,352 total and 2,361,600 trainable parameters. Section 6.1 says larger fixed-epoch subsets receive fewer steps, contradicting Section 5.1's steps-per-epoch formula; the undertraining explanation remains an author attribution.

statements.correction: Fixed 150-epoch schedule; data and compute increase together; empirical loss saturates earlier than the Kaplan reference; authors attribute the departure to incomplete convergence of larger subsets; no fitted power law or established non-bottleneck V1 test.
statements.problem: The description of this study is faithful, including its attributed undertraining explanation. Treating it as limiting V1 is unsupported because V1 already requires non-bottleneck conditions.
